title: Deterministic Validation with a Single-Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: A Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a sealed, preregistered paired experiment that measured the marginal verifier-detected effect of interposing a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial generation call per intent; that same candidate reused for both baseline and guarded episodes) we generated one candidate per natural‑language intent with gpt-5-mini for N = 250 pairs and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate) and guarded (deterministic validator; if failing, permit one automated repair). Execution completed 500 episodes with model_calls_used = 251. Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The single discordant pair was converted to pass by the single permitted repair. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the registered evidence bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being explored as intent-to-configuration translators in network operations (NetOps), promising faster authoring of device CLI sequences and intent-driven automation. Stochastic generation, however, creates operational risk: syntax errors, incorrect command ordering, local-policy violations, and vendor-CLI subtleties can produce unsafe or non-functional device changes. Empirical and survey work documents LLM feasibility for draft configurations while highlighting the continuing need for deterministic verification or human oversight [1], [2].

A widely adopted architectural response is to interpose a deterministic validator between generation and acceptance, optionally followed by bounded automated repair — a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pattern — which accepts only validator-passed candidates or attempts limited repair when mechanically verifiable defects are detected [3], [4]. Deterministic validators can check parseability, required-command ordering, touched-field constraints, and task-encoded final-state snapshots; programmatic repairs typically address syntactic or ordering defects that are mechanically resolvable.

Despite architectural adoption, the marginal verifier-detected benefit of such guardrails is rarely isolated from generation variability. To address this, we executed a preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each natural-language intent we produced exactly one initial model candidate and reused that identical candidate in both the baseline and guarded episodes. This isolates the marginal effect of (deterministic validator + up to one automated repair) on the same generated output. We report the confirmatory results from the synthetic/emulation partition (N_pairs = 250) and analyze their statistical and practical interpretation.
sections.related_work:
Prior empirical work demonstrates that LLMs can produce usable draft configurations in constrained or emulation settings; however, many studies emphasize residual syntax and semantic errors and recommend verification layers [1], [2], [5]. Tooling from the network verification community (e.g., Batfish-style analyses and header-space/model-checking approaches) provides a mature foundation for deterministic validators that check forwarding, reachability and many local-policy properties; these tools and techniques are commonly repurposed as validators in GVR pipelines [3], [6].

Research on generate-and-verify and program-repair workflows in software and configuration domains shows that automated verification plus bounded repair frequently detects and corrects mechanically checkable defects, but that semantic correctness beyond mechanically testable properties remains challenging [4], [7]. Comparative surveys of LLM self-correction emphasize fragility when self-correction lacks dependable external feedback; successful self-correction commonly relies on reliable external verifiers or highly constrained tasks [8].

Security and robustness literature documents practical prompt-injection threats to LLM-integrated systems and proposes layered defenses (filtering, detection classifiers, hardened retrieval and verifier controls), yet adaptive adversaries in NetOps workflows remain an open concern [9]. Our study situates itself at the intersection of these findings by (a) using a paired, shared_initial_candidate design that isolates verifier-and-single-repair marginal effect, (b) employing a deterministic network validator that encodes mechanical properties (syntax, ordering, final-state snapshot), and (c) archiving full validator and repair traces so numeric outcomes are auditable.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered (study_id study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1) and specified a confirmatory paired design with N_pairs = 250, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, and the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration froze the single-repair policy (at most one automated repair per episode), exclusion and contamination rules, analysis tests (exact McNemar two‑sided and paired-bootstrap percentile CIs), and a model-call budget. The preregistration artifact is archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and provider-call accounting. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one initial model-generation call was produced per intent and that identical candidate was reused for both the baseline and guarded episodes; no independent first-pass generation per condition was performed. Provider-call accounting reconciles to hosted model call events = 251, comprising 250 shared initial-generation calls plus 1 repair-stage call (model_calls_used = 251). This reconciliation is deterministic and recorded in the execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifact.

Task design and coverage. A deterministic task generator produced 250 constrained intent tasks in the emulation partition. Each task encodes: initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and a difficulty label (medium/hard/very_hard). Tasks exercised representative workflow constraints (e.g., make-before-break uplink switchover, paired-link atomic MTU changes, shutdown–configure–restore patterns) and preserved protected interfaces. The task manifest (archived) documents exact constraints used by each task; representative task payloads are included in the evidence bundle.

Guarded pipeline, validator, and repair policy. The guarded pipeline submitted the shared candidate to a deterministic network validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that: parses CLI sequences, reports parsed_command_count and required_command_count, checks required_sequence ordering and workflow constraints, computes a final_state snapshot, and emits a boolean valid flag plus violation codes when present. For guarded episodes with valid = false, the pipeline permitted up to one automated, template‑driven repair attempt limited to deterministic syntactic and ordering fixes (reorder commands to match required_sequence, split/join multi-command lines, correct obvious token-order defects). No multi-iteration repair or human escalation was permitted by design. Repair templates and their deterministic constraints were preregistered and archived.

Inclusion and contamination. The preregistered exclusion rules remove items that fail vendor-parsers such that verification cannot proceed, or items containing credential-like tokens or denylist hits. In this confirmatory run no episodes were excluded and contamination detectors flagged no confirmatory episodes: complete_pair_count = 250.

Analysis plan. The primary analysis executor was a preregistered paired binary analysis (paired_binary_analysis_v1). Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided on paired outcomes. We also computed a paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the guarded − baseline paired difference with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). All analysis parameters, inputs, and outputs are archived.
sections.results:
Execution and reconciliation. Execution completed the confirmatory partition with planned_episode_count = 500 and completed_episode_count = 500; failed_episode_count = 0 and complete_pair_count = 250. Provider-call accounting reconciles to model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared_initial_generation + 1 repair) and stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 250, repair = 1.

Primary binary outcomes and contingency. Validator-scored successes: baseline_success_count = 249 (baseline_success_rate = 0.996), guarded_success_count = 250 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The single discordant pair (baseline failed, guarded passed) corresponds to the only exercised repair call; repair-conversion rate on the confirmatory partition = 1/250 = 0.004 (0.4%).

Statistical inference. Exact McNemar (two-sided) on discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) returned p = 1.0. The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval for the guarded − baseline paired difference (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.012] (i.e., 0 – 1.2 percentage points). These values are reported exactly as produced by the preregistered analysis executor and stored in analysis/results.json.

Representative diagnostics and repair trace. Validator traces for passed episodes report parsed_command_count and required_command_count equal to the task's required_sequence length; representative scoring artifacts (for several sample tasks) show valid = true with matching parsed/required counts. The single repair trace that was executed converted a failing normalized_configuration into a validator-pass; that repair trace and the repaired candidate's validator output are archived.

Missingness, exclusions, and deviations. No episodes were excluded; all missingness counts = 0. There were no deviations from the preregistered confirmatory execution contract for the emulation partition. Deterministic reconciliation reports all consistency checks passed.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the near‑null marginal verifier effect. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the constrained synthetic/emulation partition used here, the marginal verifier-detected benefit of inserting a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair was small: the initial gpt-5-mini candidates satisfied the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases, and the guarded pipeline converted the lone failing candidate via the single permitted repair. The paired-bootstrap CI upper bound (1.2 percentage points) empirically bounds the maximum verifier-detected improvement under these pipeline and task-scope conditions.

Why the observed gain is small (artifact-grounded). The artifacts and preregistered design identify three mechanistic reasons: (1) constrained task design — required_sequences, allowed_touched_fields, and explicit intent constraints reduced ambiguity and guided generation toward well-formed CLI sequences; (2) model behavior — the declared model (gpt-5-mini) produced highly consistent, syntactically well-formed candidates for these constrained intents; and (3) validation scope — the deterministic validator is limited to mechanically checkable properties (syntax, ordering, final_state snapshot) and does not measure broader live-protocol or cross-device emergent correctness. Together these factors explain why baseline verifier-pass was high and why only one simple repair was needed.

Power and generality. The preregistration power calculation selected N_pairs = 250 assuming an emulation baseline pass ≈ 0.90 to detect a 15 percentage-point absolute production-vs-emulation contrast with ≈80% power. The observed baseline pass rate (0.996) was substantially higher than assumed; this reduces power to detect small absolute improvements in the paired contrast. Consequently, the confidence interval (0.0–1.2 pp) is the most informative quantity here: it provides an upper bound on plausible verifier-detected gains in this setting, not definitive evidence that validators are unnecessary in other contexts.

Scope, threats to validity, and operational implications. Internal validity: outcomes depend on the exact prompt templates, the single-repair policy, shared_initial_candidate semantics, and the deterministic validator encoding. Construct validity: the validator measures mechanically verifiable correctness but does not capture protocol-level dynamics or emergent multi-device behaviors. External validity: the confirmatory evidence covers only the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed in this run. Security: adaptive prompt-injection and retrieval-based adversaries were not tested.

Operational framing and recommendations. In tightly constrained emulation tasks with a capable LLM and strong task constraints, a single repair may provide limited additional verifier-detected benefit relative to always-accepting an initial candidate. This empirical result does not generalize to heterogeneous production environments, adversarial settings, multi-vendor topologies, multi-iteration repair policies, or validators that check richer properties. Practitioners should therefore regard the present result as an artifact‑grounded quantification for one narrowly defined estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics) rather than a general endorsement to remove validation or human oversight layers.

Reproducibility and auditability. All run artifacts (raw model responses, execution manifest, validator traces, repair traces, deterministic reconciliation, and analysis outputs) are archived in the evidence bundle described in the Disclosure Statement. Key numeric reconciliation facts reported above (model_calls_used = 251; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 250, repair = 1; contingency counts n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; bootstrap parameters) are reproducible from those archived manifests and are presented verbatim in the analysis artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the verifier-detected marginal benefit of deterministic validation plus one permitted automated repair on identical LLM-generated configuration candidates. In N = 250 constrained synthetic intent tasks, initial gpt-5-mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases; the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate via the single permitted repair. Observed paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp]; p = 1.0). We explicitly disclose that the preregistered sim-to-real contrast for community and production-like partitions was not executed: the executed confirmatory estimand applies only to the synthetic/emulation partition. Broader production, adversarial, multi-model, and multi-iteration repair evaluations remain necessary to establish generality. All execution and analysis manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts are archived and available in the evidence bundle described in the Disclosure Statement.

disclosure_statement:
Human role and autonomy boundary: After an autonomy lock required by the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track, the autonomous system performed literature search, study selection, preregistration freeze, prompt preservation, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, peer-review, revision, and finalization without manual human editing of technical content. A human Research Director selected the broad topic family and performed pre-lock infrastructure development only; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.

Models, tools, and framework: declared model = gpt-5-mini; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution used a guarded generate–verify–repair flow permitting at most one automated repair per episode. Provider-call accounting reconciles to model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair) with per-stage counts recorded in the archived reconciliation artifact.

Preregistration and immutable prompt reference: the study was preregistered under the stated study identifier and the immutable master prompt used to initiate the autonomous run is archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The evidence bundle contains the archived preregistration, execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts referenced in this manuscript.
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed and remain exploratory.

Deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences) but did not measure broader semantic or behavioral correctness (protocol dynamics, emergent interactions).
Single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi-model or alternate-validator generality.
Only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi-iteration repairs or human-in-the-loop escalation were not evaluated.
Adversarial and retrieval-based attacks (adaptive prompt-injection, vendor-targeted exploit vectors) and large-scale production heterogeneity were not exercised and remain open threats.
